title: The Sediment Gallery Where Kept Things Become the Only Truth

features.name: kept letter in glass
features.desc-on-touch: You find an envelope under archival glass—no sender, no date. The folded paper has become a relic, not for what it says, but for the fact of keeping itself.

features.name: photograph arranged by meaning
features.desc-on-touch: You see a photograph arranged here: a porch, a face cut off at the edge, a date hand-written on the back. The date no longer matches the world, but keeping has made it true.

features.name: stone shelf arranged by touch
features.desc-on-touch: You find seven objects arranged here, each worn smooth by a person's fingers. Their organization follows no system—only the logic of the hands that held them.

features.name: sediment reading
features.desc-on-touch: You read the strata as text. Each layer holds a kept thing—not organized, just preserved. The gallery is a slow reading of what time chose not to erase.

features.name: rust-marked metal
features.desc-on-touch: You find rust-marked metal here—a key, a fastener, something that once held things together. The rust is its truest form now, the record of years kept safe.

reverie.title: REVERIE — in the kept gallery of small things
narr: You kneel before a shelf Katita arranged years
ago—a stone, a button, a dry-cleaned envelope.
'Things prove we were here,' she said then.
Now you touch each one, and her hand is in
each arrangement. The gallery is her keeping.

inscription: to keep a thing is to refuse the world its erasure; this gallery is the archive's refusal made visible

file.name: Kept_Objects_Catalogue_Incomplete_Handwritten.txt
file.note: inventory of seven personal effects, each entry fragmentary—the archivist did not finish, or did not know how; the kept things became more true than the keeping
